BANGKOK, Oct 16 : Finance leaders of the G7 grouping agreed to hold tabletop exercises to guard against AI cyber attacks, Japanese Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said, as policymakers increasingly seek to coordinate responses to growing cyber security risks. The agreement comes after the International Monetary Fund warned this week that confidence could be undermined by an AI-enabled cyber attack on a critical service of a financial institution. Katayama's remarks to reporters on Thursday followed a meeting of finance ministers and central bank governors of the G7 advanced economies held on the sidelines of the IMF's annual gathering in Bangkok, the Thai capital. The plan will feature simulations evolved by G7 finance authorities to test how they can respond to AI-driven cyber attacks, said a Japanese finance ministry official who attended the finance leaders' meeting.

The exercises by G7 finance ministries and central banks could include private financial institutions depending on the nature of simulations, the official added. Banking regulators globally are stepping up efforts to contain growing AI risks, Reuters reported, with some pointing to the potential for cyberattacks on banks or rogue agents undermining global financial stability. Among them is the Bank of England, which is working with banks on deep cyber-recovery options, its deputy governor said on Thursday, adding that they can no longer assume their defences are immune to AI-enabled cyberattacks.

BANGKOK, Oct 16 : World Bank President Ajay Banga on Friday said the development lender has set a goal of quintupling its critical minerals business in five years, and has identified 20 countries that it can partner with on critical minerals development projects. Banga revealed the new goal in prepared remarks to a plenary session at the International Monetary Fund and World Bank annual meetings in Bangkok. "In critical minerals, we plan to quintuple our business in five years," Banga said. "This week, we launched our first country compacts with MDB partners—to build local industries and keep more jobs and value at home." The World Bank's new Metals and Minerals implementation plan is targeting $19 billion in critical minerals financing over the fiscal 2026-2030 period, compared with $3.6 billion in the fiscal 2021-2025 period.

Critical minerals development is an area where the United States, the World Bank's largest shareholder, has called for the bank to devote more financing resources. US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent said earlier this week that he wanted the bank to play a bigger role in enabling critical minerals mining and processing capacity through project de-risking and finance and investment in enabling infrastructure. He said this includes deep-sea mining projects. Banga did not mention deep-sea mining, but the bank's metals plan calls for a "precautionary approach" to the nascent sector, adding that any engagement and investments must be consistent with applicable bank policies. Banga reviewed the World Bank's overall increases in financing during the 2026 fiscal year that ended on June 30, including mobilizing $112 billion in private capital, a more than threefold increase from the 2022 fiscal year, before he assumed his role. Alongside lending from the World Bank's own balance sheet, this brought the group's total financing to $230 billion for fiscal 2026, he said.

US 10-year yield -10 bps to 5.08 per cent, curve flattens. CoreWeave and other AI corporate bonds rise.COMMODITIES/METALS: Oil mixed — Brent flat, WTI +3 per cent. Gold +1 per cent, silver +3 per cent. Today's Talking Points: Funny money The global AI trade has hit some major turbulence. South Korea's KOSPI, a top 10 global index, has lost 20 per cent of its value in barely a week, and on Thursday Japan's Nikkei slid 5 per cent. CoreWeave 2032 bonds issued just four months ago fell below 80 cents in the dollar, typically considered distressed debt levels, and the cost of insuring against major US AI firms defaulting has soared to record levels. As ever, credit markets are likely to lead equities, and the risk of a self-fulfilling doom loop cannot be ignored — selling in certain names casts a shadow over healthier credits, and downgrades and loss of investment-grade ratings could force further selling. All while cash has been spent, and capex is increasingly being financed by debt, private credit and off-balance-sheet borrowing. We're not at crisis point yet — look at the rebound in US stocks and bonds today — but vigilance is required. Bonds be bonds Incoming data shows US producer price inflation is running hotter than expected, like CPI the day before, WTI crude spikes another 3 per cent, and Treasuries rally. Sounds counterintuitive, especially given how heavily fixed income markets have traded in recent weeks, but it shows that the demise of Treasuries' safe-haven appeal has been greatly exaggerated. Thursday was one of the best days of the year for Treasuries, especially for maturities of 10 years and beyond. The question is whether this is a knee-jerk move, or will continued volatility in equities and weakness in AI-related corporate debt remind investors that the best place to hedge, diversify and protect their capital is the traditional "risk-free" asset? Guaranteed nominal yields of over 5 per cent appear to be tempting. Rotation, rotation, rotation Wall Street's resilience on Thursday was pretty remarkable, given the ferocity of the tech selloff in Asia and weight of negative sentiment at the session open. Chip stocks fell for a seventh day, their longest losing streak in four years, but the Nasdaq edged higher and, more impressively, the Dow rose 1 per cent to its highest in a month. As the US earnings season kicks into gear, the focus will be on tech. The bar of expectations is high, and if it is not hurdled, investors may decide to ramp up the rotation into other sectors. How long do rotations out of tech last? According to Deutsche Bank, since mid-2024 the average length of rotation is 67 days and the median is 59 days. In terms of tech drawdowns over these periods, the average is 16.6 per cent and the median is 14.6 per cent. NEW YORK, Oct 15 : Some current Anthropic investors and prospective investors in its upcoming initial public offering are weighing a lower valuation for the AI company after its latest financial disclosures, four people familiar with the matter said, amid broader concerns over the ballooning cost of financing AI. Some investors who attended Anthropic's investor day on Wednesday in San Francisco discussed a valuation of around $1.5 trillion, three of the people said, a significant step down from the roughly $2 trillion valuation that investors had previously expected for the November share sale. At Wednesday's meeting, Anthropic told prospective IPO investors that its third-quarter revenue jumped 45 per cent to $16.8 billion from the previous quarter, and that it was profitable on an adjusted basis during the quarter.  While those numbers assuaged some concerns about the massive costs of developing AI systems, some investors were disappointed by the slowing sequential growth rate in the latest quarter, as Anthropic's revenue more than doubled from the first quarter to $11.6 billion in the second quarter, the people added.  They spoke on condition of anonymity because they are not authorized to speak publicly on the matter.

Anthropic did not immediately respond to requests for comment.  A cooler reception for Anthropic's IPO could weigh on the wider AI market, whose near-term prospects investors see as hinging largely on the share sale's success, followed by OpenAI's potential listing next year. BELLWETHER IPO The concerns from investors come as a tech selloff is roiling global financial markets and has hurt AI infrastructure companies, chipmakers and so-called neocloud providers that rent computing power for AI broadly. Shares and bonds of Nvidia-backed CoreWeave tumbled on Thursday, reflecting growing investor concern about an AI buildout that is increasingly being financed with borrowed money. A disappointing share sale for Anthropic could further add to investor worries about the AI buildout.   The IPO market has suffered some setbacks recently, after data center operator SB Energy decided to delay its listing last month, while nuclear technology company Holtec Nuclear pulled its plans to go public.   During Wednesday's meeting at Anthropic's headquarters in San Francisco, attendees, mostly the company's most prominent investors, met with CEO Dario Amodei and finance chief Krishna Rao.  The Information earlier reported that investors were considering a lower valuation. Founded in 2021 by former OpenAI executives including Amodei and his sister Daniela Amodei, who is now Anthropic's president, Anthropic has emerged as one of the leading generative AI developers with its Claude family of models. The company's rapid growth has been underpinned by Alphabet's Google and Amazon, which are simultaneously investors, suppliers of computing power and important distribution partners, as well as AI competitors. Last year, Anthropic's revenue surged twelvefold to nearly $4.6 billion, even as the company lost more than $8 billion on an operating basis, excluding writedowns of various liabilities mostly tied to previous fundraising, Reuters reported last month. In its IPO prospectus seen exclusively by Reuters in September, Anthropic laid out a vision that AI will transform the global economy more profoundly than industrialization, electricity and the internet, even as it reported a loss of $42 billion in 2025 and projected more spending for the upcoming AI buildout.  The company has committed to spending at least $518 billion over a decade for cloud services, computing and infrastructure.

Oct 15 : Thoma Bravo-owned cybersecurity company Proofpoint will buy data security firm Varonis Systems in an all-cash deal valued at about $6.3 billion, the companies said on Thursday. Under the agreement, Varonis shareholders will receive $49.75 per share in cash, a 52 per cent premium to the company's closing share price on June 22, the day before speculation about a possible sale first emerged, the companies said.  The offer values Varonis' equity at $5.71 billion. The deal, expected to close in the first half of 2027, comes as businesses ramp up spending on cybersecurity to combat cybercrime, where AI is being increasingly used to steal data.

CoreWeave rents out computing power from Nvidia processors to companies developing and running AI, including Microsoft and OpenAI. It is one of the leading "neocloud" providers, a group of newer cloud companies that are growing rapidly to meet demand for scarce and expensive AI chips. These neocloud companies give customers access to computing power without requiring them to build their own data centers. However, supplying such capacity requires heavy upfront investment in chips and infrastructure, often financed with debt. WHAT IS ITS FINANCIAL SITUATION? The company, which has never turned a profit, has about $50 billion in debt, according to data compiled by LSEG. It raised its annual capital spending forecast by $4 billion in August to between $35 billion and $39 billion. Analysts expect revenue of nearly $13 billion this year and a loss of $2.13 billion. The yields on its bonds due in 2031, which are rated junk, have spiked to about 16 per cent, while the cost of insuring its debt against default has climbed to about 1,000 basis points, reflecting growing concern among creditors. CEO Mike Intrator told employees in an internal memo seen by Reuters that its deal backlog more than covers its debt obligations. The company had a $104.2 billion revenue backlog at the end of the second quarter, followed by more than $25 billion in new commitments early in the third quarter. Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang has also downplayed the concerns, saying CoreWeave's financial strength is improving and he sees no need to backstop it. The chip giant has agreed to buy unsold CoreWeave capacity through April 2032. WHY IT COULD BE A CANARY IN THE COAL MINE CoreWeave's business depends on two things: demand for AI computing and lenders' willingness to finance the infrastructure supplying it. But a selloff in its shares suggests a lack of confidence among investors in the latter, even as the company cites strong demand. The concern is not that AI demand will collapse, but that higher borrowing costs could make the business harder to sustain if demand were to weaken sharply. "It looks more like investors questioning how the build-out is being funded than a sudden collapse in appetite for AI computing," said Axel Rudolph, chief technical analyst at IG Group. "CoreWeave is quickly becoming the AI trade's canary in the coal mine," said Kathleen Brooks, research director at XTB. WHY ARE MARKETS FRETTING? Investors are questioning whether AI revenue can grow fast enough to cover the cost of building and financing the infrastructure. CoreWeave has to spend heavily upfront before it can collect the revenue from its contracts. Higher interest rates could drive up financing costs and further squeeze returns. The hardware itself poses another risk. Chips lose value as newer generations arrive, pushing providers to spend even more to replace them. The concerns, however, go beyond CoreWeave. US technology giants are expected to spend more than $700 billion on AI infrastructure this year. THE DOWNSIDE SCENARIO One potential consequence would be a broader financing squeeze, with lenders demanding higher returns or becoming less willing to fund other AI projects. That could force providers to scale back expansion, curbing equipment purchases and affecting the computing capacity customers expect. A setback could also deepen doubts that the AI investment frenzy is outpacing returns, piling further pressure on technology stocks. The impact of the fallout would depend on how the business is reorganized, and CoreWeave's ties to major technology companies do not, by themselves, mean its failure would trigger a wider financial crisis. WHO ELSE BEARS THE RISK? Gartner estimates about 80 per cent of neoclouds could shut down by 2030, warning that expected AI revenue will not support profitable returns on all planned infrastructure spending. Neocloud rivals Nebius, Applied Digital and Iren have fallen in the recent selloff. The cost of default protection has risen for SoftBank, which is betting heavily on OpenAI. Meanwhile, spreads for Amazon, Alphabet, Meta and Nvidia have also reached records, although they have risen much more slowly than CoreWeave's. However, these companies also have larger cash flows and stronger balance sheets.

A key sticking point between evaluators and AI labs is that information the companies might consider crucial intellectual property can also be relevant to assessing a model's risks, leading to disputes and redactions, a separate person familiar with the discussions told Reuters. The company said it cannot veto METR's findings on risks, incidents and practices, but can require narrowly defined redactions. "In line with our transparency policies, our report will openly describe the scope, access, and other limitations of our work," METR said. Evaluators at the first level will conduct narrowly scoped investigations and need approval to publish. Those at the second will receive more information and can publish without approval, subject to redactions evaluators can publicly challenge. The third, used by METR, provides employee-like access with similar publication rights to the second tier. SecureBio is in the first tier and is reviewing the chemical and biological weapons chapter of Anthropic's August risk report, having published a pilot review of the previous report. Anthropic said it would consider expanding SecureBio's access and publication rights after the review. Oct 15 : The bones of a Neanderthal from a cave in Iraq's Kurdistan region are offering evidence of both violence and compassion in the closest evolutionary cousins of our species, exhibiting a wound apparently from a fatal spear attack as well as signs of an earlier nonfatal injury that may have elicited kindly care. Researchers have discovered at Shanidar Cave in the Zagros Mountains of northern Iraq a partial skeleton of a Neanderthal, aged in the mid-40s, that included a left shoulder blade, or scapula, with a circular hole six-tenths of an inch (15 mm) wide indicative of a deeply penetrating stab. The bones of this individual, who they call Shanidar A, were unearthed from under about 25 feet (7.5 meters) of rocks and sediment inside the cave and date to about 75,000 years ago. The researchers were unable to determine Shanidar A's sex. The researchers said the injury's shape suggests it was caused by a forceful thrust using a sharpened wooden spear, a type of weapon Neanderthals are known to have used, rather than a spear with a stone tip. It was a weapon employed in hunting large mammals that were an important food source.

"The spear would have gone through the skin and major muscles, especially the pectoralis, as well as the ribcage and muscles between the ribs, and the lung," said biological anthropologist Emma Pomeroy of the University of Cambridge in England, lead author of the study published on Thursday in the journal Scientific Reports. "The location could be like the kind of 'heart shot' hunters use to kill animals quickly by puncturing the heart, but that is a bit speculative. We do see heart shots as a hunting strategy both today and in the archaeological record. Neanderthals would have known this would lead to a quick death," Pomeroy said. University of Cambridge archaeologist and study co-author Graeme Barker, who has led Shanidar Cave excavations since 2015, said the likeliest scenario is interpersonal violence. The researchers said the violence probably occurred either between members of a particular Neanderthal group or between members of rival Neanderthal groups, calling a Homo sapiens attack or an accidental injury less likely. The researchers found shards of bone displaced by the weapon. The injury indicated that the spear entered from above with a downward trajectory, penetrating the left chest cavity from the front and traveling through the body before punching the hole in the scapula, causing quick death. ANOTHER INJURY In addition to the scapula, the researchers found some ribs, a nearly complete right hand and seven teeth, mostly from the front of the lower jaw, belonging to Shanidar A. The teeth bore evidence that this Neanderthal had survived brutal injury at least a year before death — a blow to the face resulting in front teeth being smashed and lost. One tooth was split, with half remaining rotated in the mouth and others pushed out of position. "The pain would have been extreme, and basic needs like eating and drinking would have been difficult, perhaps meaning Shanidar A needed food mashing and being able to rest. It's likely that Shanidar A did need some care from members of the group for some basic needs during recovery," Pomeroy said. Shanidar A was one of five Neanderthals, four adults and one infant, whose bodies were carefully tucked behind a rock pillar in the cave in a burial cluster within a generation or so of each other. The cave was occupied by Neanderthals for tens of thousands of years as a seasonal campsite, and later by Homo sapiens. Neanderthals were more robustly built than Homo sapiens, with larger brows. They lived as hunter-gatherers and inhabited Eurasia from the Atlantic coast to the Ural Mountains from about 400,000 years ago until a bit after 40,000 years ago, disappearing after Homo sapiens became established in the region. The two species interbred, with modern non-African human populations bearing residual Neanderthal DNA. The cave, overlooking the Great Zab river valley, has been a source of information about Neanderthals since the 1950s, with Shanidar A now offering new insight into their behavior. "We see evidence of two contrasting facets of human nature – care and violence – juxtaposed in the same individual," Pomeroy said. "We see evidence all around us today that violence and care are both aspects of how we humans behave, and we see this here in Shanidar A, too. Neanderthals were like us in many respects, both the good and the bad, and this find really highlights that, going against stereotypes of Neanderthals as unintelligent, uncaring cavemen and cavewomen," Pomeroy said.

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : Japan told its G20 counterparts that authorities must watch exchange-rate moves with a high sense of urgency, Finance Minister Satsuki Katayama said on Thursday. The G20 finance leaders re-confirmed their commitment on currency policy, Katayama told reporters after attending the group's gathering, held on the sidelines of the annual IMF meetings in Bangkok this week. "I told the gathering that we must closely watch financial market developments with a high sense of urgency," Katayama said on Japan's exchange-rate policy. The remarks came as the yen's persistent weakness keeps market players on alert over the chance of another round of intervention by authorities to prop up the currency.

The G20 agrees that exchange-rate moves should be determined by markets but that excessively volatile and disorderly moves were undesirable - a line Japan points to as giving it authority to step into the market to arrest unwelcome yen swings. A weak yen has become a source of concern for Japanese policymakers by pushing up the cost of imports, including for fuel, which has spiked due to the Middle East war. Katayama said the G20 finance leaders did not produce a joint communique or a chair's statement during their meeting on Thursday. When asked about the G20 group's discussions around rising long-term interest rates, Katayama said she told the group that each country must strive to achieve its fiscal sustainability goals, but at the same time use fiscal scope to boost investment in growth areas. .

BANGKOK, Oct 15 : The United States wants its global partners to rename artificial intelligence as "super intelligence," convinced that the new moniker better reflects the emerging technology, a top US Treasury official told Reuters in an interview on Thursday. Treasury Undersecretary for International Affairs Erin Browne said Washington was in negotiations with other shareholders of the International Monetary Fund about using the new term in a statement being drafted by the fund's steering committee, the International Monetary and Financial Committee. US President Donald Trump last month directed US government agencies to use the words "super intelligence" instead of "artificial intelligence" when referring to the technology. Browne said the United States, which holds the rotating presidency of the Group of 20 major economies, wanted the change to take hold internationally as well.

"President Trump has been really clear on this, and he's, you know, using the term SI, and I think it's a clear priority for the US to use that term, and we think that more appropriately encapsulates the technology at hand," Browne said. She declined to comment on whether Washington would refuse to sign off on the statement unless the switch was made. "We're still in the middle of negotiations on that statement, so I'm not going to, you know, sort of run ahead of that," she said. A source familiar with the matter said US officials had suggested during meetings on the IMFC statement that they would insist on the new language, raising eyebrows among some other IMFC members. If Washington withholds its support for a consensus statement, the current IMFC chair, Saudi Finance Minister Mohammed Al-Jadaan, could still issue a so-called chair's statement summarizing the views of the members. One possibility might involve skipping a mention of SI or AI and focusing on "new technology" instead, the source said. The IMFC will hold a news conference and release any agreed statement led by Al-Jadaan and IMF Managing Director Kristalina Georgieva on Saturday. "We see this as a driving force behind American growth and global growth," Browne said. "Many countries are looking to the US to set the standards, as well as to set the path forward for SI development and how that can really enhance and boost growth and productivity on a global basis."

Oct 15 : Anthropic should delay its US IPO until it addresses concerns about safety, governance and the pace of development, urged New York City Comptroller Mark Levine in a letter to the AI lab's CEO Dario Amodei. AI systems have advanced rapidly over the past 12 months, outpacing regulation and drawing scrutiny over potential risks, including safety, cybersecurity threats and misuse. "Instead of proceeding headlong with its IPO, the company should focus its energies on addressing these unprecedented risks," Levine wrote in the letter seen by Reuters on Thursday. NYC's public pension funds have a combined $7 million in exposure to Anthropic through private equity holdings, the comptroller's office told Reuters.
